scenario.brief:
Two branches in `insights-app` passed review this morning and you are the release captain for today.

`feature/search` was started from the current `main` and `main` has not moved since, so its two commits can slide straight onto `main`. `feature/metrics` was branched earlier; since then Tomasz landed a dependency bump on `main`, so the two lines of history have diverged.

Merge them in this order, watching the graph on the right as you go:

1. Merge `feature/search` into `main`. Expect a **fast-forward**: no new commit, `main` simply moves.
2. Merge `feature/metrics` into `main`. Expect a **three-way merge**: Git creates a merge commit with two parents.

The two features touch different files, so there is nothing to resolve by hand. Finish on `main` with a clean working tree.
scenario.whyItMatters: Knowing which shape a merge will produce before you run it is a mark of fluency. Fast-forwards keep history linear; merge commits record that two lines of work were integrated. Teams pick conventions (`--no-ff`, squash) based on exactly this distinction.

objectives.title: Merge feature/search into main as a fast-forward
objectives.description: main should move to the search commits without creating a merge commit.
hints: You merge into the branch you are on. Check `git branch` first. A fast-forward happens when the current branch is an ancestor of the branch being merged.
`git merge feature/search` while on main. The output will say "Fast-forward" and the graph stays a straight line.
Run `git switch main` (if needed) then `git merge feature/search`

objectives.title: Merge feature/metrics into main with a merge commit
hints: main and feature/metrics have both moved since they split, so Git needs a commit that has both as parents.
`git merge feature/metrics` finds the common ancestor, combines both sides and, with no conflicts, commits automatically with a default message.
Run `git merge feature/metrics`. Then `git log --oneline --graph` shows the merge commit with two parent lines.

objectives.title: End on main with a clean working tree and no merge in progress
hints: Both merges complete on their own because the branches changed different files.
`git status` should say nothing to commit. If it mentions a merge in progress, finish it with `git commit` or back out with `git merge --abort`.

debrief.summary: You performed both kinds of merge and saw how the starting shape of the history decides whether Git moves a pointer or creates a new commit.
internals: For feature/search, Git found that main's commit was an ancestor of the search tip. Nothing needed combining, so it moved the ref `main` forward and updated the index and working tree. No commit was created.

For feature/metrics, Git computed the merge base (the last commit both sides share), diffed each side against it, and combined the two diffs. Since they touched different files, the result was automatic.
The merge commit stores two parents: the previous main tip first, then the metrics tip. `git log --graph` draws the second parent as a line joining from the side.
Both branches still exist and point where they did; merging never moves the branch being merged in.

keyCommands.note: Force a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible; some teams require this for traceability.
The shape of history, including merge commits.
Delete a branch whose commits are already merged.

commonMistakes: Merging while on the wrong branch (for example merging main into feature/search).
Expecting a merge commit after a fast-forward and thinking something went wrong.
Being surprised that the merged branch still exists. Merging copies nothing and deletes nothing; it only moves the current branch.
debrief.atWork: Hosted platforms offer "merge", "squash" and "rebase" buttons that map exactly onto these shapes. Knowing what each produces lets you read any team's history and choose the right option for a pull request.
debrief.interview: "Explain fast-forward versus three-way merge" is a staple. Mention the ancestor check and the merge base, and that a fast-forward creates no commit.
